content.value:
This is the capstone. Build a complete OpMode with everything you've learned across all five modules — subsystems, commands, PID + feedforward, voltage compensation, Pedro Pathing, Zones, and loop-time monitoring.

You'll create two subsystems: one for the drivetrain and one for an arm mechanism. The arm uses a motor and a servo. You'll bind gamepad controls, follow a PathChain on a button press, and make the robot react automatically to field position.

You may use AI for conceptual help, but NOT for writing code — that defeats the whole purpose. Of course, in the real world, it is recommended that you use AI (although sparingly and intelligently).

The robot needs an arm mechanism with these capabilities:

A motor named arm_motor that extends the arm up and down.

A servo named hand_servo that opens and closes to grab game elements.

Arm motor must use MotorEx with tuned PID coefficients (P, I, D).

Voltage compensation must be applied so the arm behaves the same regardless of battery level.

Put all constants — motor type, arm positions, servo positions, nominal voltage, PID/FF coefficients — in a separate config file. Refer to those constants from the subsystem; never use magic numbers.

The robot needs a mecanum drive subsystem with these capabilities:

Four motors — front_left_motor, front_right_motor, back_left_motor, back_right_motor — wrapped in MotorEx.

A Follower created inside the subsystem from Constants.createFollower(hardwareMap). Call follower.update() in periodic() — not from the OpMode. The subsystem owns the Follower.

A drive method that accepts forward, strafe, and turn inputs and gives it to the follower.

A stop method that sets all four motors to zero.

A method to accept a PathChain and tell the Follower to follow it.

An 18-inch square robot PolygonZone synced to the follower's pose in periodic(). Expose a way to check whether this zone overlaps another Zone.

All input must go through GamepadEx with SolverLib bindings — never read gamepad values inside a loop.

Y button: arm moves up.

A button: arm moves down.

Right bumper: hand closes (grab).

Left bumper: hand opens (release).

Joystick driving set as the drive subsystem's default command using a RunCommand.

When the B button is pressed, the robot must follow a PathChain.

The PathChain must have at least two segments — drive up and then strafe right — starting near field center.

Use BezierLine segments, constant heading interpolation, and global deceleration.

The button handler calls the drive subsystem's path-following method. The Follower lives in the subsystem and updates in periodic() — the OpMode only triggers the path.

Find the red alliance base zone coordinates. This is a rectangular area on the field where the red alliance parks. Use the Pedro Pathing Visualizer to find the coordinates.

Create a PolygonZone for it.

When the robot enters the red base zone, the arm must raise. When the robot exits, the arm must lower.

Use two Triggers — one for enter, one for exit — against the robot zone from the drive subsystem. No manual state tracking. The Trigger handles edge detection.

Override run() in the OpMode — call super.run() first so the scheduler runs, which calls all subsystem periodic() methods (including the Follower update).

After super.run(), measure and display the loop time in milliseconds using ElapsedTime. Reset the timer after each measurement.

Display a warning in telemetry if the loop time exceeds a 50ms budget.

End each iteration by calling telemetry.update().

Run the OpMode and verify every requirement:

Drive with joysticks — mecanum should work with voltage compensation applied.

Press Y and A — arm moves up and down.

Press bumpers — hand opens and closes.

Press B — robot follows the PathChain autonomously.

Drive into the red base zone — the arm raises automatically. Drive out — the arm lowers.

Loop time displays in telemetry every tick. It should stay well under 50ms in the simulator. On real hardware, it would stay under budget if you used bulk reads and MotorEx caching.
